studies.title: Divergent impacts of explainable AI for dermatological diagnosis on clinicians versus lay people
studies.finding: Task: giving a top-three differential diagnosis from clinical photographs of skin conditions. The study focused on atopic dermatitis, pityriasis rosea, Lyme disease and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, with images balanced across light and dark skin tones. AI system: a deep learning model trained to perform evenly across skin tones, shown with one of four kinds of explanation (prediction only, heatmap, similar example images, or a multimodal large language model's written explanation). Humans: 153 primary care physicians (PCPs) diagnosed each image first on their own and then again with AI help. The paper also tested 320 medical students on the same task and 623 lay people on a simpler melanoma-versus-mole task. Main result: without AI, PCPs had 11.5 ± 1.4% top-1 accuracy and 16.1 ± 1.8% top-3 accuracy; with AI suggestions, top-1 accuracy rose by 21.5% and top-3 by 43.5%. When the AI was wrong, the PCPs' final answers barely changed, but medical students and lay people relied on the AI more. The written LLM explanations helped PCPs the least. Main limitation: this was a simplified online experiment with only 12 images per participant and no patient history. The authors also chose the images on purpose so the AI was right about 79% of the time, which does not reflect how the model would behave in real use.

studies.title: Interval cancer, sensitivity, and specificity comparing AI-supported mammography screening with standard double reading without AI in the MASAI study: a randomised, controlled, non-inferiority, single-blinded, population-based, screening-accuracy trial
studies.design: population-based randomised controlled non-inferiority trial
studies.ai_system: Transpara, used to triage exams to single or double reading and to support detection
studies.humans: Screening radiologists in the Swedish programme. Arms: AI-supported screening vs standard double reading without AI. 105,934 women randomised 1:1 (53,043 vs 52,872).
studies.finding: The primary outcome was the interval cancer rate after at least two years of follow-up. It was 1·55 (95% CI 1·23–1·92) per 1000 with AI-supported screening and 1·76 (1·42–2·15) per 1000 with standard double reading, a proportion ratio of 0·88 that met non-inferiority. The AI arm had fewer invasive (75 vs 89), T2+ (38 vs 48) and non-luminal A (43 vs 59) interval cancers, and the authors report higher sensitivity.
studies.limitation: The primary analysis was powered for non-inferiority, not superiority, and was run in one Swedish screening programme with one AI product.

studies.title: Ambient AI Scribes in Clinical Practice: A Randomized Trial
studies.design: pragmatic three-group randomised clinical trial
studies.ai_system: Microsoft Dragon Ambient eXperience (DAX) Copilot and Nabla ambient AI scribes
studies.humans: 238 outpatient physicians from 14 specialties at one academic health system, randomised 1:1:1 to DAX, Nabla or usual care
studies.finding: The primary outcome was the change from baseline in log writing time-in-note. Nabla users had a 9.5% decrease (95% CI −17.2% to −1.8%; P=0.02) versus control, while DAX users showed no significant change (−1.7%; 95% CI −9.4% to +5.9%; P=0.66). Both scribes improved Mini-Z scores (DAX +2.83; Nabla +2.69).
studies.limitation: Scribes were used in only about 30% of visits (33.5% DAX, 29.5% Nabla) over a two-month period at a single health system.

studies.title: Performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
studies.design: six-experiment comparison including blinded evaluation of real emergency department cases
studies.ai_system: OpenAI o1 series (o1-preview), compared with GPT-4 and physician baselines
studies.humans: Hundreds of physicians at different training levels across the experiments; two attending physicians in the real-world emergency department experiment
studies.finding: o1 was compared with physicians on diagnosis and management reasoning, from published vignettes to 76 real emergency department cases at three decision points. At initial triage, o1 placed the correct or a very close diagnosis in 67.1% of cases, compared with 55.3% and 50.0% for the two attending physicians. Across experiments the authors report that the model outperformed physicians and older models.
studies.limitation: The real-world arm compared the model with only two physicians on 76 text-only cases from one centre, and several tasks used curated vignettes.

studies.title: Large language model diagnostic assistance for physicians in a lower-middle-income country: a randomized controlled trial
studies.design: single-blind randomised controlled trial with clinical vignettes
studies.ai_system: GPT-4o
studies.humans: 60 licensed physicians in Pakistan (58 completed), all after a 20-hour AI-literacy course
studies.finding: On up to 6 vignettes, physicians with LLM access plus usual resources had a mean diagnostic reasoning score of 71.4%, versus 42.6% with usual resources alone. The adjusted difference was 27.5 percentage points (95% CI 22.8 to 32.2), and time per case was similar. In an exploratory analysis the LLM alone beat LLM-assisted physicians by 11.5 percentage points (95% CI 5.5 to 17.5).
studies.limitation: Small vignette-based study of physicians given intensive AI-literacy training, which may not generalise to untrained clinicians or real patients.

studies.title: Automation Bias in Large Language Model–Assisted Diagnostic Reasoning among Physicians Trained in AI Literacy — A Randomized Clinical Trial
studies.design: single-blind randomised clinical trial (automation bias)
studies.ai_system: ChatGPT-4o, with deliberately erroneous suggestions in 3 of 6 vignettes for the treatment arm
studies.humans: 44 physicians in Pakistan who had completed a 20-hour AI-literacy programme
studies.finding: Physicians diagnosed six vignettes. The treatment arm got deliberately wrong LLM suggestions in some cases; the control arm got error-free ones. Mean composite diagnostic accuracy was 73.3% with wrong suggestions versus 84.9% in controls, an adjusted reduction of 14.0 percentage points (95% CI −18.9 to −9.1; P<0.0001). Top-choice accuracy was 76.1% versus 90.5%.
studies.limitation: Small vignette trial in which LLM errors were planted by the investigators, so the error rate does not reflect real-world LLM output.

studies.title: Computer-Assisted Colonoscopy in High–Adenoma Detection Rate Settings in a High-Risk Population: A Randomized Clinical Trial
studies.design: multicentre randomised clinical trial
studies.ai_system: Computer-aided detection (CADe) system for colonoscopy
studies.humans: Senior and junior endoscopists in a high adenoma detection rate setting, performing 1356 randomised colonoscopies
studies.finding: CAD-assisted colonoscopy met non-inferiority for adenoma detection rate against standard colonoscopy (58.5% vs 53.3%), but superiority was not statistically significant overall. Gains appeared only in an exploratory FIT-positive subgroup (65.3% vs 57.4%; P=.02), driven mainly by diminutive adenomas, and CAD led to more intensive surveillance recommendations.
studies.limitation: Enrolment of 1356 fell short of the planned 1480, and the surrogate endpoint (ADR) does not show any effect on cancer prevention.

studies.title: Artificial intelligence assisted colorectal lesion detection in private practices a randomized controlled study
studies.design: prospective multicentre randomised controlled trial in private practices
studies.ai_system: EndoMind real-time polyp detection system
studies.humans: Highly experienced endoscopists in private endoscopy centres across Germany doing screening and surveillance colonoscopy (number of endoscopists not confirmed)
studies.finding: The primary endpoint was mean adenoma detection rate. It was 32.9% with traditional colonoscopy and 34.5% with computer-aided colonoscopy (p = 0.656), with no significant difference in the intention-to-treat analysis.
studies.limitation: Control-group ADR was higher than assumed in the power calculation, so the trial may have been underpowered to detect a small benefit.

studies.title: Randomized Controlled Trial of Large Language Model–Assisted Diagnostic Accuracy in Nephrology
studies.design: online randomised open-label parallel-group trial (research letter)
studies.ai_system: GPT-5
studies.humans: 97 residents and board-certified physicians, mostly nephrologists and mostly French, giving 556 case evaluations
studies.finding: On complex open-ended nephrology vignettes, top-3 diagnostic accuracy was 57.5% with AI versus 37.2% without (adjusted OR 2.8, 95% CI 1.5–5.2). Top-1 accuracy was 51.5% versus 33.0% (adjusted OR 2.7). GPT-5 alone reached 77.1% on the same benchmark, well above AI-assisted clinicians.
studies.limitation: Short research letter on fixed vignettes, not powered for subgroups, with a largely French volunteer sample.

studies.title: Diagnostic capability of large language models in critically ill patients: a prospective single-centre study comparing ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini with emergency physicians
studies.design: prospective single-centre observational diagnostic agreement study
studies.ai_system: ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Pro
studies.humans: Emergency physicians caring for 180 critically ill emergency department patients (number of physicians not stated)
studies.finding: Diagnoses were compared stage by stage on real critically ill ED cases. Physicians had the reference diagnosis in their top-5 preliminary list in 83.9% of cases and their top-3 differential in 98.3%, significantly better than every LLM (all p < 0.001).
studies.limitation: The reference diagnosis was the physicians' own final diagnosis, which biases the comparison in the physicians' favour.

studies.title: Comparing Ophthalmologist and Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Responses to Patient Questions
studies.design: retrospective cross-sectional comparison of written responses
studies.ai_system: ChatGPT (GPT-4o)
studies.humans: 41 board-certified ophthalmologists answering on the AAO 'Ask an Ophthalmologist' forum (250 questions sampled)
studies.finding: Ophthalmologist evaluators rated the accuracy of answers to patient eye-health questions on a 7-point Likert scale. ChatGPT and ophthalmologist answers had similar mean accuracy (5.8 [SD=1.1] vs 5.5 [SD=1.1], p=0.07), and evaluators preferred ChatGPT in 49.5% of cases. Ophthalmologist answers were easier to read (grade 11.0 vs 12.7, p<0.001).
studies.limitation: Forum answers were written asynchronously by volunteers years earlier, so they may not reflect clinicians' best effort or real clinical communication.

studies.title: Improving Diagnostic And Management Accuracy In Hard-To-Diagnose Pigmented Skin Lesions With Interactive And Interpretable AI Assistant For Dermatoscopy: Results From A Two-Phase Reader Study
studies.finding: Task: classify dermoscopic images of pigmented skin lesions into seven diagnosis groups and choose what to do next (dismiss, biopsy or treat, or follow up). AI: idea®, an interactive decision-support platform that detects and highlights dermoscopic patterns and, once the physician has reviewed them, gives a rule-based diagnosis grounded in established dermoscopic criteria. Humans: 16 physicians with proven dermoscopy experience read 208 images, first without the tool and then, after a washout of at least 14 days, with it. On the 49 hard lesions (cases misclassified or read with low confidence without the tool), the share correctly called malignant or benign rose from 50.6% without AI to 69.3% with AI (p < 0.001), correct diagnosis from 28.3% to 45.0% (p < 0.001), and correct management from 53.0% to 64.8% (p = 0.02). The biggest limitation: this was a non-randomised, before-and-after reader study on images rather than real patients. The second phase was deliberately weighted toward hard lesions, and the key results apply to that subset, not to every lesion.

studies.title: Impact of LLM assistance on physician decision-making: a multi-country randomized controlled trial
studies.finding: Physicians worked through standardised clinical vignettes to test their clinical decision-making. Physicians given access to GPT-4o were compared with physicians who had no AI access. The parallel-group randomised trial enrolled 249 physicians in Indonesia, Kenya and the Netherlands. Physicians with GPT-4o access scored higher on the vignettes in every country. The gap was 18 percentage points in Kenya (95% CI 12.7 to 23.2, p < 0.001), 10.7 percentage points in Indonesia (95% CI 5.7 to 15.7, p < 0.001) and 7.2 percentage points in the Netherlands (95% CI 3.7 to 10.7, p < 0.001). The main limitation is that this was done with written cases under controlled conditions, not with real patients. The control group was also not allowed to use the internet or clinical guidelines, and harms were not assessed. The paper is an early peer-reviewed version that may still be edited before the final version.

studies.title: Large language models improve physician accuracy but lead to false reliance
studies.finding: In this preprint, physicians answered clinical cases with and without help from an AI assistant. The AI was CORA, an agentic large language model built by researchers led by the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) in Heidelberg, which pulls in sources and shows citations for its answers. Among the 46 physicians in the study, accuracy rose from 70.8% unaided to 82.6% with CORA. The citations cut both ways: when they appeared to back a correct answer, physicians took the advice 76.9% of the time, up from 34%, but when they appeared to back a wrong answer, physicians' resistance to that answer fell from 92% to 34.8%. The most important limitations are that the preprint has not been peer reviewed and that 46 physicians were tested on study cases, not on real patients in live care.

studies.title: Radiologists, LLMs fail at spotting AI-generated chest x-rays
studies.source: AuntMinnie (reporting a study in the Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine)
studies.finding: The task was sorting 160 chest X-rays into real (40) or AI-generated (120, made by three different image-generation pipelines). Three large language models (Gemini 3.5 Flash, GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 Sonnet) were compared with four human readers from a Seoul National University Hospital team: two radiologists and two general practitioners. On the main measure, balanced accuracy, the top performers were Gemini 3.5 Flash at 77.9% and one radiologist at 75.8%, with no statistically significant difference between them, while the general practitioners performed near chance. Humans were better at spotting images made by diffusion models (82% to 100% vs 32% to 72% for the LLMs), and the LLMs were better at correctly calling real images real (90% to 100% vs 50% to 100%). The main limitation is size: only four human readers and 160 images, on a task about checking image authenticity rather than making a diagnosis. These figures come from a trade-press report of the peer-reviewed paper.

studies.title: AI-based clinician decision support system for diagnosis of inherited retinal diseases: a multicenter, randomized trial
studies.finding: The task was to predict which of 17 genotype categories caused a suspected inherited retinal disease, using retinal images (colour fundus photographs and OCT scans), before genetic test results were available. The AI was Retina4IRD, a Vision Transformer tool pretrained with RETFound. In a multicentre randomised controlled trial, 300 patients were randomised 1:1 to retinal specialists working with Retina4IRD or specialists working alone; 295 had sequencing results and were analysed. The abstract does not say how many specialists took part. On the primary outcome, top-5 genetic accuracy, the AI-assisted arm scored 88.5% and the specialist-only arm 67.3% (P < 0.001), and top-1 accuracy was 37.8% versus 22.4%. The most important limitation is that the trial measured whether the predicted genotype category matched sequencing, not patient outcomes; the finding that management decisions were better with AI came from a post hoc analysis.

studies.title: Comparative Cost of Care Recommended by Large Language Models versus Treating Physicians
studies.finding: The task was writing an assessment and plan from the clinical presentation in de-identified outpatient and emergency department notes. The orders in each plan were then priced using the 2026 Medicare fee schedules. The AI side was 24 systems (20 general-purpose large language models and 4 specialized medical systems), each given the same 200 cases. The human comparison was the plan actually documented by each case's treating physician; the number of physicians is not stated in the authors' public materials. On the main measure, cost of care, a Nature research highlight of the paper reports that LLM-suggested plans were three times as costly as physicians' plans, driven by more tests, referrals and medications. The most important limitation is that this was a retrospective study of documented notes rather than real-time care, and higher cost alone does not show whether the extra orders helped or harmed patients.

studies.title: Sequential diagnosis with language models
studies.finding: The task was step-by-step diagnosis. Researchers turned 629 published NEJM case records and emergency department encounters into interactive cases where you ask questions and order tests, and each test adds to an estimated cost. The AI was Microsoft's Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO), running on GPT-5. It was compared with practising generalist physicians, who worked through a 56-case subset of the complex NEJM cases. Depending on its test budget, the AI reached the correct diagnosis in 79.6% to 84.5% of cases. Physicians averaged 22.3% without reference tools and 36.1% with them, and even the best physician (51.8%) was beaten by the AI on both accuracy and cost. The main limitation is that these were simulated, text-only cases built from past records, not real patients. The AI could not examine anyone, the cases were hard ones given to generalists, and the authors, who work at Microsoft, say it still needs testing in real clinical practice.

studies.title: Clinicians vs. artificial intelligence in patient outcome prediction in the intensive care unit
studies.finding: The task was predicting outcomes for ICU patients: in-hospital and 30-day mortality, acute kidney injury, delirium, and ICU and hospital length of stay. The AI was a set of prediction models trained on 46,631 ICU admissions. In the retrospective arm, seven clinicians predicted outcomes for 990 admissions from patient data alone. In the prospective arm, clinicians made predictions for 238 admissions during active care, while the AI worked from data extracted for the same admissions. The preprint version reports that 75 clinicians made at least one prediction, across 15 adult ICUs in Alberta, Canada. The abstract reports the results as direct comparisons rather than headline numbers. In the retrospective arm, AI generally beat individual clinicians, but the pooled predictions of all seven clinicians beat the AI. In the prospective arm, subspecialised physicians generally beat the AI, while physicians in training and nurses generally did worse than it. Combining clinician and AI predictions often gave the best results. The main limitation is that the real-world prospective arm was small (238 admissions) and confined to one Canadian province's ICUs, and the AI saw extracted data rather than the bedside picture the clinicians had.

studies.title: Performance of Clinical AI System and Physicians and Frontier Language Models in primary care diagnostics
studies.finding: The task was to run adaptive primary-care consultations, asking questions before choosing a diagnosis, a workup and initial treatment, across 150 synthetic Polish-language cases. The AI was Doctorina, a clinical AI system, which was also compared with four standalone frontier language models. The human comparison group was eight physicians. Doctorina's Top-1 diagnostic concordance was 82.0% against 57.0% for the physicians (difference 25.0 percentage points; 95% CI 17.7–32.7), and its primary-or-reference-differential concordance was 97.3% against 85.0%. Across 149 case pairs, normalized workup scores were 89.4 against 66.9 and treatment scores were 83.7 against 61.2. The main limitation is that the cases were synthetic consultations, not real patients, and only eight physicians took part. This is also a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and its authors include Doctorina's co-founder and staff.

studies.title: Clinician-centered evaluation of large language model-generated discharge summaries for longer hospitalizations
studies.design: Paired blinded comparison of LLM-generated vs human-authored discharge summaries
studies.ai_system: A large language model; the specific model could not be confirmed from the abstract
studies.humans: Human-authored discharge summaries from 60 Internal Medicine hospitalisations lasting 7 to 21 days, rated in pairs by hospitalists and primary care physicians (number of raters not confirmed)
studies.finding: Clinician reviewers compared LLM-generated and human-authored discharge summaries for 60 longer Internal Medicine stays. They preferred the LLM-generated summaries for 95% of encounters and rated them higher for quality, readability, factuality and completeness. PCPs rated the LLM summaries as better for understanding and communicating hospital care and for follow-up care; of 31 radiology incidental findings the LLM identified, 93.5% were rated factually correct and 87.1% appropriate for reporting.
studies.limitation: Only 60 hospitalisations from one internal medicine setting were used, and the outcome is clinicians' ratings and preferences, not downstream patient outcomes or errors in care.

studies.title: Assessing AI and Neurologist Diagnostic Reasoning Against Neuropathological Ground Truth
studies.finding: Task: give a ranked top-three differential diagnosis from written case summaries of complex neurological illness, scored against the diagnosis confirmed at autopsy. The AI was DIAGNO, an LLM-based system built on GPT-4o that rates its own confidence and looks up references for cases where its confidence is lower. The humans were three board-certified neurologists, each with more than 10 years in practice; every case was read by just one of them, and they could use resources such as UpToDate. On 203 complex Massachusetts General Hospital cases, DIAGNO's top-3 accuracy was 0.67 against the neurologists' 0.63, and its accuracy by disease category was 0.74 against 0.67. None of the comparisons by disease category was statistically significant, and the authors describe DIAGNO's performance as comparable to the neurologists'. The main limitation is that this was a retrospective study of selected written summaries rather than full records or real patients, and it is a preprint; GPT-4o was also one of the three blinded judges scoring the answers.

studies.title: Performance of artificial intelligence versus clinician left-ventricular segmentation of cardiac MRI for mortality prediction: a retrospective, multicentre, prognostic study
studies.finding: The task was outlining the left ventricle on cardiac MRI to measure ejection fraction, and then using those measurements to predict death from any cause. A deep-learning segmentation tool was compared with expert clinicians' segmentation of the same scans from 27,382 consecutive patients at UK and US centres. Over a median follow-up of 5.6 years, 3,458 patients (13%) died. AI-derived ejection fraction predicted death marginally better than clinician-derived ejection fraction (C index 0.669 vs 0.637, and 0.781 vs 0.777 after adjusting for age and sex). The main limitations are that the study was retrospective, that it measured how well each set of numbers predicted death rather than any effect on care, and that the gain after adjustment was very small.

studies.title: From dusk till dawn?—Night shift-induced fatigue, diagnostic performance, and AI assistance in chest radiography
studies.finding: The task was reading bedside chest radiographs for five findings: cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, pleural effusion, pulmonary opacities and atelectasis. Residents read with and without help from an AI model built at Aachen University Hospital, which pre-filled a structured report that they could accept or change. Ten radiology residents (mean experience 35 months) each read sets of 33 radiographs before and after a first-call on-site night shift, and the morning after the shift they read both with and without AI. Accuracy was measured as Cohen's κ against an expert majority vote. Six residents classed as fatigued by eye tracking fell from κ = 0.71 ± 0.05 to κ = 0.61 ± 0.10 after the shift (p < 0.001), and non-fatigued readers fell from κ = 0.72 ± 0.03 to κ = 0.65 ± 0.03 (p = 0.037). AI help did not significantly improve accuracy (Δκ = 0.03–0.04; p ≥ 0.525) and did not restore pre-shift performance, although it significantly shortened reporting time in non-fatigued readers (Δ9.9 s; p = 0.031). The main limitation is size: 10 residents at a single centre, using one in-house AI model on a set of test radiographs rather than live clinical reporting.

studies.title: Comparing Physician and Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Responses to Patient Questions Posted to a Public Social Media Forum.
studies.design: Cross-sectional study of 195 Reddit r/AskDocs exchanges, blinded evaluation in triplicate
studies.ai_system: ChatGPT
studies.humans: Verified physicians who answered 195 questions on a public forum; responses rated by a team of licensed health care professionals
studies.finding: The task was answering patient questions posted to a public social media forum (Reddit's r/AskDocs). ChatGPT's answers were compared with answers from verified physicians to 195 questions, and a team of licensed health care professionals rated each pair blind, in triplicate. Evaluators preferred the chatbot response in 78.6% (95% CI, 75.0%-81.8%) of the 585 evaluations. Good or very good quality was 78.5% (95% CI, 72.3%-84.1%) for the chatbot vs 22.1% (95% CI, 16.4%-28.2%) for physicians, and empathetic or very empathetic was 45.1% (95% CI, 38.5%-51.8%) vs 4.6% (95% CI, 2.1%-7.7%). The physician answers were forum posts, not clinical care, and they were much shorter (52 [17-62] words vs 211 [168-245] words).
studies.limitation: Physician answers came from a public online forum rather than clinical care, and chatbot responses were much longer.
studies.check_note: The JAMA page only showed the abstract and front matter, so I checked against the abstract; the numbers match, and I added the CIs and the word counts.

studies.title: AI-enabled electrocardiography alert intervention and all-cause mortality: a pragmatic randomized clinical trial.
studies.design: Pragmatic multisite randomized controlled trial of AI-ECG mortality-risk alerts delivered to physicians
studies.ai_system: AI-enabled ECG alert (AI report plus warning messages flagging patients predicted to be at high risk of death)
studies.humans: 39 physicians caring for 15,965 hospitalized patients
studies.finding: The task was spotting hospitalized patients at high risk of death, with 90-day all-cause mortality as the outcome. The AI-ECG alert sent an AI report and warning messages to physicians, flagging patients predicted to be at high risk of death. The trial involved 39 physicians and 15,965 patients, and physicians who got the alerts were compared with physicians who did not. Mortality was 3.6% in the intervention group versus 4.3% in the control group (HR = 0.83, 95% CI = 0.70-0.99); the benefit was mainly in patients with high-risk ECGs (HR = 0.69, 95% CI = 0.53-0.90), whose cardiac death was 0.2% versus 2.4% (HR = 0.07, 95% CI = 0.01-0.56). Only 39 physicians were randomized, and how the alerts reduced deaths is not yet known.
studies.limitation: Only 39 physicians were randomized, and the mechanism of the benefit is unclear.
studies.check_note: Checked against the PubMed abstract text (via search, as the direct page did not load): I added the number of physicians (39) and patients (15,965), the HR for high-risk ECGs, and the 95% CI for cardiac death; the other numbers match.

studies.title: Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.design: Single-blind randomized clinical trial using clinical vignettes
studies.ai_system: LLM (GPT-4)
studies.humans: 50 physicians (26 attending physicians and 24 residents) in family, internal or emergency medicine; 25 randomized to the LLM plus conventional resources and 25 to conventional resources only
studies.finding: Physicians worked through up to 6 clinical vignettes and were scored on a structured diagnostic reasoning rubric. One group could use an LLM (GPT-4) along with conventional resources, and the other group used conventional resources only. There were 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents), 25 in each arm. The median diagnostic reasoning score per case was 76% with the LLM vs 74% with conventional resources (adjusted difference 2 percentage points, 95% CI -4 to 8; P = .60), while the LLM on its own scored 16 percentage points (95% CI, 2-30; P = .03) higher than the conventional resources group. The study was small and used vignettes rather than real patients.
studies.limitation: Small sample of 50 physicians working on vignettes rather than real patients.
studies.check_note: Only part of the journal full text loaded: Table 1 confirmed 50 participants (26 attendings, 24 residents; 25 per arm), which were added to humans and finding; the outcome numbers are as screened and the Results section was not readable in the fetched page, so they should be rechecked.

studies.title: Comparison of Ophthalmologist and Large Language Model Chatbot Responses to Online Patient Eye Care Questions.
studies.design: Cross-sectional masked panel evaluation
studies.ai_system: ChatGPT
studies.humans: AAO-affiliated ophthalmologists who wrote the forum answers; masked panel of 8 board-certified ophthalmologists as raters
studies.finding: The task was answering 200 patient eye care questions posted on an online medical forum. ChatGPT answers were compared with answers written by ophthalmologists affiliated with the American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO), and a masked panel of 8 board-certified ophthalmologists rated both. Chatbot answers were as likely as the ophthalmologists' answers to contain incorrect or inappropriate material (prevalence ratio [PR], 0.92; 95% CI, 0.77-1.10). The two sides were also similar for likelihood of harm (PR 0.84) and extent of harm (PR 0.99), and raters told AI from human answers with a mean (SD) accuracy of 61.3% (9.7%). The answers came from an online forum (posts dated 2007-2016) rather than real clinical care, and they were judged by ophthalmologists, not patients.
studies.limitation: Answers came from an online forum rather than real clinical care, and they were rated by ophthalmologists, not patients.
studies.check_note: I checked this against the abstract on the JAMA Network Open page; the full text was not available, and the abstract text I got stopped after the PR 0.92 result, so the harm PRs (0.84 and 0.99) come from the screening record and are not independently re-checked, but all other figures match.

studies.title: Prospective Evaluation of AI Triage of Pulmonary Emboli on CT Pulmonary Angiograms.
studies.design: Prospective single-centre before-after study (two sequential phases)
studies.ai_system: Commercially available AI triage system for PE detection on CTPA
studies.humans: 42 radiologists in total: 31 read without AI (phase 1) and 37 read with AI (phase 2), with 26 of the 42 reading in both phases
studies.finding: Radiologists looked for pulmonary embolism on CT pulmonary angiograms in routine practice, first without AI (503 studies) and then with AI (1023 studies), with re-review by thoracic radiologists as the reference standard. The AI was a commercially available triage system that flags studies with suspected PE. There were 42 radiologists: 31 in the no-AI phase and 37 in the AI phase, and 26 of them read in both phases. Accuracy and miss rate for any PE were 97.6% and 12.3% without AI and 98.6% and 6.1% with AI, which was not significantly different (P = .15 and P = .11), and examination and report turnaround times did not improve; only the mean wait time for PE-positive studies improved, falling from 21.5 minutes without AI to 11.3 minutes with AI (P < .001). The two phases ran one after the other at a single centre rather than being randomised, and only some of the radiologists took part in both.
studies.limitation: The phases were sequential and not randomised, the study took place at one centre, and the radiologists only partly overlapped between phases.
studies.check_note: All numbers matched the PubMed abstract; I added the radiologist counts (31, 37, 26 of 42) and the finding that turnaround times did not improve, but could not open the full text (RSNA/DOI fetch failed).

studies.title: From tool to teammate in a randomized controlled trial of clinician-AI collaborative workflows for diagnosis.
studies.design: Randomized controlled trial using clinical vignettes
studies.ai_system: Custom LLM-based collaborative diagnostic system that synthesises independent clinician and AI assessments
studies.humans: 70 clinicians
studies.finding: Clinicians worked through up to six clinical vignettes in one hour to reach a diagnosis. They used either conventional resources or a custom LLM system that combined the clinician's and the AI's independent assessments, with the AI giving either the first opinion or a second opinion. Seventy clinicians took part, and two blinded board-certified physicians graded the answers. Diagnostic accuracy was 85% with AI as first opinion and 82% with AI as second opinion, against 75% with conventional resources; neither was statistically different from AI alone (90%). The cases were vignettes, not real patients.
studies.limitation: Performance was measured on clinical vignettes under time limits, not in real patient care.
studies.check_note: Added the 70 clinicians, the vignette-based design and blinded grading (taken from the PubMed abstract and figure legend; the PMC full text was blocked) and rewrote the finding in the required order.

studies.title: A large language model for complex cardiology care.
studies.design: Randomized controlled trial using retrospective patient data
studies.ai_system: AMIE (Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer), an LLM-based experimental medical AI system
studies.humans: 9 general cardiologists; 3 blinded subspecialist raters
studies.finding: General cardiologists assessed the triage, diagnosis and management of 107 complex real-world cases of suspected genetic cardiomyopathy. Each case was done twice, once with and once without help from the AMIE large language model. Nine general cardiologists took part, and three blinded subspecialists rated the work using a ten-domain rubric. Subspecialists preferred AMIE-assisted assessments 46.7% of the time versus 32.7% for cardiologists alone (P = 0.02), with 20.6% rated as a tie; cardiologists alone had more clinically significant errors (24.3% versus 13.1%, P = 0.033) and more missing content (37.4% versus 17.8%, P = 0.0021). The study used only nine cardiologists and retrospective records, not live care.
studies.limitation: Only nine cardiologists assessed retrospective cases from a single subspecialist practice rather than providing live care.
studies.check_note: The numbers match the paper; added the 107 cases and three blinded subspecialist raters from the Nature Medicine article page.

studies.title: Detecting structural heart disease from electrocardiograms using AI.
studies.design: Model development with internal/external validation, a controlled comparison with cardiologists, and a prospective clinical trial
studies.ai_system: EchoNext deep learning ECG model
studies.humans: Cardiologists (number not given in abstract)
studies.finding: The task was detecting many forms of structural heart disease from ECGs. EchoNext is a deep learning model trained on more than 1 million heart rhythm and imaging records. In a controlled evaluation, cardiologists (number not given in the abstract) read the same ECGs. The abstract says the model outperformed cardiologists but gives no numbers. The comparison could not be checked against the full text.
studies.limitation: The available abstract gives no figures or cardiologist numbers for the AI-versus-cardiologist comparison.
studies.check_note: The Nature page showed only the abstract, which matches the record; the editors should pull the full text to add the comparison numbers and the number of cardiologists.

studies.title: Assessment of a Large Language Model's Responses to Questions and Cases About Glaucoma and Retina Management.
studies.design: Single-center comparative cross-sectional study
studies.ai_system: GPT-4 (version dated May 12, 2023)
studies.humans: 15 participants from Mount Sinai–affiliated eye clinics: 12 board-certified, fellowship-trained subspecialists (8 glaucoma, 4 retina) and 3 ophthalmology trainees (2 fellows, 1 senior resident). 13 participants rated the responses while masked to their source.
studies.finding: Clinicians and GPT-4 answered 20 patient questions and managed 20 deidentified glaucoma and retina cases (10 of each per specialty), and the responses were rated on Likert scales for accuracy and completeness. GPT-4 (version dated May 12, 2023) was compared with 12 fellowship-trained attendings (8 glaucoma, 4 retina) and 3 trainees. Against glaucoma specialists, GPT-4 had a higher combined mean rank for accuracy (506.2 vs 403.4; P < .001) and for completeness (528.3 vs 398.7; P < .001). Against retina specialists, accuracy did not differ significantly (235.3 vs 216.1; P = .17), but GPT-4 ranked higher for completeness (258.3 vs 208.7; P = .005). The study was single-center, measured one time point and used one group of attendings and trainees.
studies.limitation: Single-center, single-time-point study with one group of attendings and trainees and a small set of 20 questions and 20 cases.
studies.check_note: Added the participant breakdown (8 glaucoma and 4 retina attendings, 2 fellows and 1 senior resident; 13 masked raters) and the missing glaucoma completeness result (528.3 vs 398.7, P < .001), and changed the limitation to the one the authors state; all other numbers matched the full text.

studies.title: Prospective validation of dermoscopy-based open-source artificial intelligence for melanoma diagnosis (PROVE-AI study).
studies.design: Prospective observational study; dermatologists estimated melanoma probability before and after seeing real-time AI scores
studies.ai_system: ADAE ("All Data Are Ext"), the open-source top-ranked algorithm of the 2020 SIIM-ISIC Challenge, applied to dermoscopy images
studies.humans: 11 dermatologists recruited patients; 5 dominant dermatologists (mean 16 years post-residency experience) enrolled 97% of lesions
studies.finding: For skin lesions already scheduled for biopsy to rule out melanoma, dermatologists estimated the probability of melanoma before and after seeing the score from ADAE, an open-source dermoscopy AI. 435 participants contributed 603 lesions (95 melanomas), and they were recruited by 11 dermatologists, 5 of whom enrolled 97% of lesions. On its own, ADAE had an AUC of 0.857, higher than the dermatologists' AUC before seeing the AI (0.780; p = 0.007). At its predetermined threshold ADAE had a sensitivity of 96.8% (95% CI: 91.1–98.9%) and a specificity of 37.4% (95% CI: 33.3–41.7%). The dermatologists' AUC improved from 0.7798 to 0.8161 after seeing ADAE (p = 0.042), but the study was a non-randomised before/after comparison in a population that was 96% White.
studies.limitation: Non-randomised before/after design within one study, limited to lesions already selected for biopsy, with 96% White participants and most lesions from 5 dermatologists.
studies.check_note: Changed comparison to 'both' because the paper also compares ADAE alone with dermatologists before AI (AUC 0.857 vs 0.780, p = 0.007), and added the dermatologist numbers (11 recruiting, 5 enrolling 97% of lesions); the journal page cut off before the Discussion, so the limitation is taken from the Results and abstract.

changes.text: This edition rebuilds each section around ten highly cited studies added to the register, published from 2023 onwards. They include the first randomised evidence that AI alerts to physicians can be linked to lower mortality [S26], an earlier trial in which LLM access did not help physicians [S27], prospective studies in pulmonary embolism triage [S29] and melanoma [S34], and the patient-question studies [S25][S28]. It also adds three newer studies: a neurology comparison against autopsy-confirmed diagnoses [S22], cardiac MRI mortality prediction [S23], and residents reading chest X-rays after night shifts [S24].

This edition adds ten studies, including the first randomised trial on real patients outside screening and endoscopy, in inherited retinal disease, a multi-country trial of LLM help on written cases, and new evidence that citations can drive false reliance on AI. It also adds studies on the cost of AI-written care plans, step-by-step diagnosis on simulated cases, ICU outcome prediction, LLM-written discharge summaries, dermoscopy decision support and detection of AI-generated X-rays, which broaden the picture beyond diagnosis while keeping it mixed.

This is the first edition. It covers 11 studies published between November 2025 and August 2026: screening and procedural trials in mammography and colonoscopy, LLM diagnostic trials on vignettes and real emergency department cases, an automation-bias trial, ambient scribes, patient communication and AI-assisted skin diagnosis.

title: AI vs Physician: how AI is changing what physicians can do
summary: The strongest evidence on real patients still comes from a few trials of clinicians using AI: AI-ECG alerts to physicians were followed by lower 90-day mortality in hospitalised patients [S26], and AI-supported mammography was at least as safe as double reading [S2]. Other real-world tools showed no clear gain in accuracy, including pulmonary embolism triage [S29], colonoscopy detection aids [S7][S8] and chest X-ray reporting after night shifts [S24]. On written cases, large language models (LLMs) alone often score as high as or higher than physicians [S18][S20][S22][S27][S30], and LLM help raised physicians' scores in most recent trials [S5][S9][S13][S30], though not in an earlier one [S27]. Comparisons on real patients remain split [S4][S10][S19], and wrong or citation-backed AI advice can pull physicians into errors [S6][S14].
key_findings: In a pragmatic randomised trial with 39 physicians and 15,965 hospitalised patients, AI-ECG mortality-risk alerts were followed by fewer deaths at 90 days (3.6% vs 4.3%), although it is not known how the alerts produced this effect [S26].

Results of AI help on real patients depend on the task: AI support improved breast screening [S2], prediction of the genetic cause of inherited retinal disease [S16] and dermatologists' melanoma assessment [S34], but did not clearly improve pulmonary embolism detection [S29] or colonoscopy adenoma detection [S7][S8].

On written or simulated cases, an LLM working alone often matched or beat both unaided and AI-assisted physicians [S5][S9][S18][S27][S30], but this has not been shown in live care, and one prospective emergency study on real critically ill patients found physicians ahead [S10].

Giving physicians an LLM did not raise diagnostic reasoning scores in an early 2024 trial [S27], whereas later trials found gains on vignettes [S5][S9][S13][S30] and on retrospective cardiology cases with fewer clinically significant errors [S31].

Blinded raters judged chatbot answers to patients' online questions to be as accurate as [S11][S28], or better and more empathetic than [S25], clinicians' forum answers, but those answers were forum posts and not clinical care.

Physicians follow AI errors: deliberately wrong LLM suggestions lowered diagnostic accuracy by 14 percentage points [S6], and citations attached to wrong answers made physicians far less likely to resist them [S14].
AI-generated care plans for documented cases cost about three times as much as treating physicians' plans, mainly because of more tests, referrals and medicines [S17].

sections.heading: AI on its own against clinicians
paragraphs: Several well-cited studies compare AI output directly with clinicians' output, mostly on curated material rather than in live care. On 603 real skin lesions already booked for biopsy, an open-source dermoscopy algorithm had an AUC of 0.857, against 0.780 for dermatologists' own estimates [S34]. At its set threshold it caught 96.8% of melanomas but had a specificity of only 37.4% [S34]. A deep learning ECG model was reported to outperform cardiologists at detecting structural heart disease, but the available abstract gives no figures [S32]. GPT-4 answers to glaucoma questions and cases ranked higher than glaucoma specialists' answers for accuracy and completeness. Against retina specialists, accuracy did not differ, though GPT-4 ranked higher for completeness [S33]. This was a single-centre study using 20 questions and 20 cases [S33].

Text-based diagnostic studies favour the models, but nearly all of them use written or simulated cases. A diagnostic system built on GPT-5 solved 79.6% to 84.5% of simulated sequential cases, against 22.3% to 36.1% for generalist physicians [S18]. A commercial primary-care system beat eight physicians on synthetic consultations in a preprint written partly by the company's own staff [S20]. In a large prior study, GPT-4 alone also scored above physicians using conventional resources on vignettes [S27]. Against autopsy-confirmed diagnoses in 203 complex neurology cases, an LLM-based system was comparable to experienced neurologists (top-3 accuracy 0.67 vs 0.63, not significant) [S22]. That study is a preprint, and GPT-4o was one of its judges [S22].

On real patients, the results are split. On 76 real emergency cases, o1 placed the right diagnosis at triage more often than two attending physicians [S4]. In a prospective single-centre study of 180 critically ill patients, however, emergency physicians beat every LLM tested [S10]. That study used the physicians' own final diagnosis as the reference, which favours the physicians [S10]. In ICU outcome prediction, AI generally beat individual clinicians on records. In live care, subspecialised physicians generally beat the AI, while trainees and nurses generally did worse than it [S19]. On 27,382 cardiac MRI scans, AI-measured ejection fraction predicted death marginally better than clinicians' measurements, with very little difference after adjusting for age and sex [S23].

sections.heading: Clinicians working with AI
paragraphs: The study with the most direct link to patient outcomes is a pragmatic randomised trial of AI-ECG alerts. Physicians who received alerts flagging high-risk patients had lower 90-day mortality among their patients (HR 0.83) [S26]. The benefit was concentrated in patients with high-risk ECGs [S26]. Only 39 physicians were randomised, and how the alerts led to fewer deaths is unclear [S26]. A population-based randomised trial of more than 105,000 women also found that AI-supported mammography screening met non-inferiority for interval cancers against standard double reading, with fewer invasive interval cancers [S2]. A multicentre randomised trial in 300 patients found that retinal specialists using an AI tool predicted the genetic cause of inherited retinal disease more accurately (top-5 accuracy 88.5% vs 67.3%) [S16].

Other real-world studies of clinicians working with AI found no clear benefit. In a prospective single-centre before-and-after study, AI triage of CT pulmonary angiograms did not significantly change accuracy or miss rate [S29]. Turnaround times did not improve either, although waiting time for scans positive for pulmonary embolism fell from 21.5 to 11.3 minutes [S29]. Two randomised colonoscopy trials found no significant overall gain in adenoma detection [S7][S8]. In a small single-centre study, AI-prefilled chest X-ray reports did not restore residents' accuracy after night shifts [S24].

A recurring finding on written cases is that clinicians working with AI do not reach the score of the AI alone. With a model alone scoring higher still, the LLM-assisted physicians scored no better than controls in one trial [S27], and LLM-assisted physicians and specialists scored below the model alone in others [S5][S9]. A workflow that combined the clinician's and the AI's independent assessments raised accuracy to 82% to 85%, against 75% with conventional resources. The AI alone scored 90%, which was not statistically different [S30]. Pooling clinician and AI predictions often gave the best results in ICU outcome prediction [S19].

sections.heading: Reading images and other pattern tasks
paragraphs: The imaging evidence is the most mature, but it is uneven. The strongest positive result is the large Swedish mammography trial [S2]. That trial used one AI product in one programme and was powered for non-inferiority, not superiority [S2]. In dermatology, one prospective study on real patients found that dermatologists' AUC for melanoma rose from 0.780 to 0.816 after seeing the AI score [S34]. That study was non-randomised, and 96% of participants were White [S34]. Two image-based reader studies point the same way, with large gains for primary care physicians [S1] and gains on hard pigmented lesions [S12]. Both used curated images rather than patients [S1][S12].

Several studies of detection and triage aids found little or no benefit. Pulmonary embolism triage did not significantly improve accuracy [S29], and colonoscopy aids did not clearly improve adenoma detection, particularly where baseline detection was already high [S7][S8]. One colonoscopy trial also found the AI led to more intensive surveillance recommendations [S7]. For ECGs, AI detected structural heart disease [S32] and flagged mortality risk [S26]. On a different kind of task, the best LLM and the best radiologist were similar at telling real from AI-generated chest X-rays, while general practitioners performed near chance [S15]. That study had only four readers and 160 images [S15].

sections.heading: Diagnosis, reasoning and management
paragraphs: On written vignettes, trials of LLM help have moved from no effect to consistent gains. In a 2024 trial with 50 physicians, GPT-4 access did not improve diagnostic reasoning scores (76% vs 74%) [S27]. Later trials found sizeable gains: 27.5 percentage points among AI-trained physicians in Pakistan [S5], 7 to 18 points across Indonesia, Kenya and the Netherlands [S13], and higher accuracy in nephrology [S9]. A collaborative workflow also raised accuracy [S30], as did an agentic LLM that cited sources [S14]. All of these used written cases. The control arms in one trial could not use the internet or guidelines [S13], and the nephrology trial was a short research letter [S9].

Management evidence is thinner but growing. In a randomised study using retrospective records of 107 complex suspected genetic cardiomyopathy cases, subspecialists preferred assessments made with LLM help over those by general cardiologists alone [S31]. The unaided assessments had more clinically significant errors (24.3% vs 13.1%) and more missing content [S31]. Only nine cardiologists took part [S31]. In ophthalmology, GPT-4 answers to management cases ranked well against specialists [S33]. Measured by cost, however, LLM plans for 200 documented cases were about three times as expensive as treating physicians' plans [S17]. That study could not say whether the extra orders helped or harmed patients [S17].

sections.heading: Communication and documentation
paragraphs: Two well-cited cross-sectional studies compared chatbot answers with clinicians' answers to patients' online questions. On a public forum, blinded health professionals preferred ChatGPT's answers in 78.6% of evaluations and rated them far more often as good quality and as empathetic [S25]. The physicians' answers were short forum posts, about a quarter the length of the chatbot answers [S25]. For eye care questions, chatbot answers were as likely as ophthalmologists' answers to contain incorrect or inappropriate material, and similarly likely to cause harm [S28]. A later study found similar accuracy, with ophthalmologists' answers easier to read [S11]. None of these studies involved real clinical encounters, and patients did not rate the answers [S25][S28][S11].

For documentation, a pragmatic three-arm randomised trial of ambient scribes found that one product cut note-writing time by 9.5% while the other had no significant effect [S3]. Both scribes improved a measure of physician well-being, but they were used in only about 30% of visits [S3]. Clinicians preferred LLM-written discharge summaries for 95% of 60 longer hospital stays [S21]. That outcome was preference ratings, not errors in care or patient outcomes [S21].

sections.heading: Training, examinations and skill
paragraphs: No study in this review tests AI in examinations or measures how skills develop over time. Some studies do compare clinicians by training level. In ICU outcome prediction, subspecialised physicians generally did better than the AI, while physicians in training and nurses generally did worse than it [S19]. When a dermatology AI was wrong, primary care physicians' answers barely changed, but medical students relied on it more [S1]. Fatigue after a night shift lowered radiology residents' accuracy, and AI help did not restore it [S24].

Training in AI use was not enough to protect against AI errors. Two trials in Pakistan gave physicians 20 hours of AI-literacy training. LLM help raised their scores [S5], but deliberately wrong suggestions still lowered their accuracy by 14 percentage points [S6].

sections.heading: Risks: over-reliance, lost skill and bias
paragraphs: Over-reliance on AI is documented on written cases. Planted LLM errors cut physicians' diagnostic accuracy [S6]. When citations appeared to support a wrong answer, physicians' resistance to that answer fell from 92% to 34.8% [S14]. Less experienced users followed wrong dermatology AI advice more than primary care physicians did [S1]. No study in this review measured whether clinicians lose skill over time from using AI.

Other risks include more downstream care and gaps in who the tools were tested on. AI help was linked to more intensive surveillance after colonoscopy [S7], higher-cost care plans [S17], and, for one melanoma algorithm, low specificity at its set threshold [S34]. Bias evidence is limited. One study deliberately balanced light and dark skin tones [S1], while the prospective melanoma study enrolled a population that was 96% White [S34]. AI-generated medical images can also fool general practitioners [S15].

sections.heading: Where this is heading
paragraphs: This section is interpretation, based on trends in the cited studies. First, the evidence is shifting from vignettes towards real patients and outcomes. A trial now links AI alerts to lower mortality [S26], a randomised trial links AI-supported screening to fewer interval cancers [S2], and prospective real-patient studies have appeared in dermatology, radiology and emergency care [S10][S29][S34]. These remain few, often single-centre, and mixed in result.

Second, study designs are moving from 'AI as a tool' towards structured collaboration and pooled judgement. In these designs, clinician and AI judgements are combined [S19][S30] or the AI drives the diagnostic workup [S18]. On written cases, AI alone often still matches or beats clinician-AI teams [S5][S9][S30]. Third, the risks being studied are moving from accuracy alone to automation bias, citations that make wrong answers look credible, and cost [S6][S14][S17]. On current evidence, these trends do not show that AI improves outcomes across routine practice.

open_questions: Do the gains seen on written cases from LLM help [S5][S9][S13][S30] carry over to real consultations with real patients?
How did AI-ECG alerts reduce mortality [S26], and would the effect hold in other hospitals and with more physicians?
Does regular use of AI change clinicians' unaided skills over time, especially for trainees, who relied on AI more when it was wrong [S1]?
Do higher-cost AI care plans [S17] and more intensive surveillance [S7] lead to better patient outcomes, or to over-investigation?
Which ways of presenting AI advice reduce automation bias without losing its benefits [S6][S14][S30]?
How well do imaging and dermatology tools perform in more diverse populations than those studied [S34]?
